source: Herbert Weir Smyth, Greek Grammar, read at https://grammata.pages.dev/ (college section numbers). Meanings are Smyth's glosses where he gives one.

nouns.note: Smyth's Attic paradigm is θάλαττα, with ττ, not θάλασσα.

verbs.note: Same uncontracted vowel type as λῡ́ω (§376 a). Smyth prints παιδεύω and παιδεύουσι (§423) and ἐπαίδευον, ἐπαίδευσα, and the pluperfect stem ἐπεπαιδεύκη (§429). The other parts follow that stem, the reduplication of §440, and the recessive accent of §423.

§607 glosses παύω as make cease, and the middle παύομαι as cease. The parts follow λῡ́ω (§369, §440, §423). §489 b notes that a sigma in the aorist of παύω is a later form in the manuscripts, so the aorist passive here is ἐπαύθην.
§441 prints the perfect πεφόνευκα and the gloss murder. §607 glosses the same verb as slay.
§441 prints κεχόρευκα. An initial aspirate is reduplicated by the smooth stop (§441).
§607 glosses βασιλεύω as am king, and names it as a denominative of βασιλεύς. The parts follow παιδεύω.
§607 glosses the active βουλεύω as consult, and the middle βουλεύομαι as deliberate. Reduplication of β is βε-, as in βέβλαφα (§440).
§808 lists θεραπεύω with the gloss tend. Initial θ is reduplicated by τ (§441).
§819 glosses πιστεύω as trust. The parts follow the uncontracted vowel type of παιδεύω (§376 a, §607).
§607 glosses θῡ́ω as sacrifice. §500 gives υ long in the present. §441 prints the perfect τέθυκα, with υ short, as in λέλυκα beside λῡ́ω (§374). §588 prints the aorist passive ἐτύθην.

§489 prints κελεύω order, κεκέλευσμαι, ἐκελεύσθην, with σ added. §489 a says that other verbs in -ευω form the aorist passive in -θην, without σ. The perfect active κεκέλευκα was not printed in the sections read.
The aorist passive in §369 is the second aorist ἐγράφην, not a first aorist.

§545 prints ἔπεμψα and ἐπεμψάμην, and glosses πέμπω as send. The future πέμψω has the same ψ. §478 and §569 print the second perfect πέπομφα. The perfect middle and the aorist passive were not printed in the sections read.
εἰμί has only the present and future systems (§768). There is no Attic aorist and no perfect.

adjectives.class: first and second, three endings, feminine α after ρ
first and second, three endings, feminine ᾱ after ι

adjectives.note: Listed at §287 with the adjectives declined like ἀγαθός. Oxytone, so the accents sit where they sit in ἀγαθός.
Listed at §287 with the adjectives declined like ἀγαθός.

added_step2.note: Proclitic (§179). With the genitive only. ἐξ before a vowel, ἐκ before a consonant (§136).
With the genitive only. The acute becomes a grave before the noun (§154).
With the dative only. In Attic prose outside Xenophon, μετά with the genitive is the usual word.
The items use the accusative, for motion toward (§1695.3).
With the genitive of the personal agent and a passive verb (§1698.1.b).
With the genitive of the people ruled. The present ἄρχει follows the thematic ending of §383. Principal parts are not added here.
A copulative conjunction. It joins words, clauses, or sentences.
A strongly adversative conjunction, stronger than δέ.
Postpositive (§2803). Causal γάρ is a conjunction.
The emphatic forms are ἐγώ, ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ. The short forms μου, μοι, με are enclitic.
A cry. With the genitive of cause: φεῦ τοῦ ἀνδρός.

Feminine, declined like χώρᾱ (§216). Smyth prints ἡμέρᾱ, ἡμέρᾱς, ἡμέρᾱν, and ἡμέραις. The dative singular ἡμέρᾳ is that declension’s dative. The dative of time when usually has an attributive (§1539).
Masculine, second declension, like ἵππος (§231). Smyth prints the genitive λίθου, the genitive plural λίθων, and the dative plural λίθοις as the means.

added_step3.note: The orthotone forms include σύ, σοῦ, σοί, and σέ. The enclitic forms are σου, σοι, and σε. An enclitic does not stand first (§187 a).

Smyth prints the declension at §327. The neuter nominative and accusative are αὐτό. In an oblique case, standing alone, it means him, her, it, or them, and Attic uses it instead of οὗ, οἷ, ἕ (§328 b).
A verb of will. It takes the infinitive (§1991). Smyth prints βούλεται (§1996).
Attic prose. θέλω is poetic. It takes the infinitive. Smyth prints ἐθέλειν (§1991).
A verb of ability takes the infinitive. Smyth prints οὐκέτι ἐδύνατο … βιοτεύειν, and also δυνάμεθα with an infinitive (§1154) and δύναται with an infinitive (§3007).

added_step3b.note: Gender and number come from the antecedent, and the case comes from the use in its own clause (§2501). The forms below are the §338 table, without the dual.
As because, ὅτι takes the indicative for a fact (§2241). After λέγω it introduces a statement in the indicative (§2577, §2017 b).
A simple present or past condition has εἰ with the indicative (§2291). The negative of the protasis is μή (§2286).
The ordinary Attic prose form of εἰ with ἄν. It takes the subjunctive (§2283, §2291). It is not the conjunction of a simple indicative condition.
With the subjunctive after a primary tense. After a secondary tense, the optative or the subjunctive (§2196). The negative is μή.
Negative of purpose (§2193), of a condition (§2286), and of a fear clause (§2221). With ὥστε and the infinitive the negative is generally μή (§2251).

οὐ before a consonant, οὐκ before a smooth vowel, οὐχ before a rough vowel (§137). Negative of a causal fact (§2240) and of ὥστε with a finite verb (§2251). In a fear that something may not happen, οὐ follows μή (§2221).
With the infinitive, a natural result (§2258). With the indicative, an actual result (§2257).
οὕτω before a consonant, οὕτως before a vowel (§136).

In classical Greek φημί almost always takes the infinitive, with the subject in the accusative when it is a different person (§2017 a, §2016, §1975). Smyth prints φησί and φησὶ (§2016) and ἔφη. No other forms are added.
Active λέγω with ὅτι or ὡς means say and takes the indicative (§2017 b, §2577). Smyth prints λέγει (§2614). Active λέγω with the infinitive means command (§2017 b).
A verb of thinking almost always takes the infinitive (§2580, §2016). Smyth prints νομίζω (§2576).

Printed at §2224 and §2225. A fear that something may happen takes μή with the subjunctive after a primary tense (§2221, §2225). The optative after a primary tense is rare (§2227). No further forms are added.
